body: Wednesday, March 05 2025 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto
Information available before 2025-03-05 00:00 UTC. Prices use completed prior sessions. Prepared retrospectively; later outcomes are excluded.

Macro Stance: US growth is being repriced, not inflation. The Canada and Mexico tariffs took effect after Trump locked them in, and US stocks tumbled as they were confirmed [1][2]. CNBC reports that stagflation fears are rising as the tariffs take effect and the economy slows [3], and the Wall Street Journal calls the combination a two-headed monster stalking the economy [4]. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker had first-quarter growth at negative 1.5 percent [5], weekly jobless claims jumped to 242,000 [6] and consumer confidence posted its biggest drop since 2021 [7]. February manufacturing ISM printed 50.3 with growth slowing more than expected [8][9]. Prices are not the immediate constraint: January PCE inflation was 2.5 percent, in line with forecasts [10], and the Fed's favourite core gauge hit 2.6 percent [11]. Equities confirm the growth worry: the S&P 500 closed at 5,778.15, down 1.2 percent in the prior session and 3.6 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04).

Rates & Curve: The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.22 percent and the 2-year is 3.96 percent at the prior close, a 10Y-2Y spread of +26 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-04). Over 20 observations the 2-year is down 30 bps from 4.26 percent and the 10-year is down 32 bps from 4.54 percent, so the spread has narrowed by only 2 bps. The curve is positively sloped and the 20-observation move is a bull flattening. The 10Y-3M spread is still -12 bps against a 4.34 percent three-month bill, and the 30-year at 4.53 percent keeps the long end 31 bps above the 10-year. This is a growth-led rally, not a dovish Fed: Reuters reports that parts of the Treasury market are worried about a pause in rate cuts [12], and Cleveland's Hammack is urging patience on further cuts [13]. The dollar index is at 105.74 index points, down 2.98 percent over 20 sessions, and the VIX rose to 23.51, up 26.3 percent over 20 sessions and 21.0 percent over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04; US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-04).

New / Most Important: The most important item is a split in the headlines that the market is hedging rather than resolving. Commerce Secretary Lutnick said the Canada tariffs are just getting started [14], while CNBC reported that Trump could scale back the Canada and Mexico tariffs on Wednesday [15]. A second risk sits inside government: the administration disbanded two expert panels on economic data [16], and the Commerce Secretary's comments on federal data raised fears of interference [17]. Democrats are serious about a shutdown [18], and CNN reports they rejected the GOP funding strategy [19]. Data credibility and shutdown risk arrive together, which is why the bond market is buying duration and equities are not.

Playbook ✓: Stay light on high-beta US growth into the Wednesday tariff decision. Own the 10-year as the hedge while it trades below the 4.54 percent level of 3 February, and use VIX calls rather than outright shorts while the VIX sits at 23.51. Change the call if the 10-year closes back above 4.54 percent with the S&P 500 holding 5,778.15: that would mean the bond bid is fading and the stagflation trade has won the argument. A shutdown that drags on pushes the same logic toward defensive staples.

Macro Stance: Europe is the one major market where policy is moving the other way. Germany's parties agreed to reform the debt brake, and the euro and stock futures rallied on the news while bonds fell [20]; economists are reacting to the deal [21] and the key details are a fiscal-rule change and an infrastructure splurge [22]. Brussels is adding to it: the EU chief unveiled an €800bn plan to rearm Europe [23], and the Commission proposed €150 billion of loans for pan-European defence [24]. European indices closed at a record on Monday, led by defence shares [25], and Germany's DAX passed 23,000 for the first time [26]. The DAX then closed at 22,326.81 in the prior session, down 3.5 percent on the day the US tariffs took effect (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04).

Credit & Inflation: The ECB is in a holding pattern with a dovish tilt. Reuters' Morning Bid says the ECB may stumble into stimulus [27], and its own calls are getting harder [28]. Euro-area inflation eased slightly in February [29] and unemployment was 6.2 percent [30], so the bank has little reason to hurry. The currency is the cushion: EUR/USD closed at 1.0485, up 1.53 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). Investors had been betting on the sharpest US-Europe inflation divergence since 2022 [31], and the euro's gain now looks like a fiscal story rather than a price story.

New / Most Important: Defence is the trade, and it is now a policy trade. Thales and BAE soared after the $840 billion rearmament plan [32], but European arms makers warn that filling the Ukraine gap will take time [33]. Autos are the other side of the same policy. European auto stocks sank as US tariffs on Mexico and Canada kicked in [34], while the Commission agreed to water down automotive emission targets [35]. The carmakers feel the tariffs first and get the regulatory relief second.

Playbook ✓: Own European defence and infrastructure builders on dips, and keep the autos underweight against the tariff tape. The fiscal call changes if the German reform stalls [20] or if the euro gives back its 1.53 percent 20-session gain while Bund yields keep rising, which would mean the bid is not spreading beyond defence. Watch the ECB's stimulus talk as well: a dovish turn would weaken the euro, help exporters and dent the defence premium at the margin.

Macro Stance: China's February data are steadier than the tariff backdrop. Manufacturing reached a three-month high [36] and factory activity picked up even as trade uncertainty weighed [37]; the Guardian reported a return to growth despite the threat of higher tariffs [38]. The demand side is softer: Hong Kong's January retail sales fell 3.2 percent [39], and consumer inflation was 0.5 percent in January while producer deflation persisted [40][41]. The trade shock is now concrete rather than rhetorical, and Beijing has answered with its own extra tariffs of 10 to 15 percent on US farm products [42]. The Economist frames the deflation question as a moment of truth for Xi Jinping [43], and that policy test is harder to pass while the trade shock lands.

PMIs & Activity: The official non-manufacturing PMI was 50.4 in February [44], and the manufacturing reading reached a three-month high, which may be the pre-tariff peak [36]. The China Beige Book expects US tariffs could dent the manufacturing sector in the second half [45]. The US side is losing momentum too: the American ISM manufacturing print of 50.3 came in weaker than expected [8][9]. The forward risk is therefore a synchronised slowdown in the two largest factory economies, not a China-specific cycle.

Credit Impulse: Credit is the weak link, and the central bank is managing it quietly. Reuters reports the property loan contraction has eased after government support [46], and sources say Chinese banks are heeding the PBOC's call to cut dollar deposit rates [47]. That is liquidity management rather than a credit boom. The state remains the marginal lender in property, which is why the housing data move more slowly than the equity tape.

Property: Property is still shrinking, but the decline is narrowing. The decline in second-hand home prices narrowed for a seventh straight month in February [48], while a Reuters poll sees prices dropping further and no recovery until 2026 [49]. The state is propping up the market [50], and hedge funds are betting on a turnaround in the unloved sector [51]. Hong Kong's version of the stress is distress expected as Winland sells assets [52], and New World Development flagged an interim loss of up to $875 million amid China's property woes [53].

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Policy is leaning into the trade fight. Beijing will impose tariffs of up to 15 percent on some US goods from March 10 [54], after hitting US soybeans and lumber [55] and US farm products with duties of 10 to 15 percent [42]. It has also put 15 US companies on its export-control list [56] and banned imports of Illumina's gene sequencers [57]. On currencies, Trump says China and Japan cannot keep reducing the value of their currencies [58], but Reuters reports the evidence for a cheap yuan is unfounded [59]. Steel capacity is the structural lever: China announced plans for steel output cuts to restructure the industry [60].

Markets & Flows: Equities are running ahead of the data. The Hang Seng closed at 22,941.77, down 0.28 percent in the prior session but up 10.35 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). China internet ETF KWEB is up 10.88 percent over 20 sessions at 34.24 dollars, and the large-cap ETF FXI is up 10.47 percent at 35.04. The Shanghai Composite is at 3,324.21 index points, up 2.26 percent over 20 sessions, and the CSI 300 ETF ASHR is up 2.5 percent at 26.61 dollars. The yuan is weaker: USD/CNY closed at 7.2843, up 1.24 percent over 20 sessions. Retail appetite is visible in the Hong Kong listings: Mixue surged 43 percent on its debut [61]. The mainland A-share ETF is the slower, more domestic gauge, and it has risen far less than Hong Kong's internet names, with ASHR up 2.5 percent over 20 sessions against KWEB's 10.88 percent.

New / Most Important: Export controls have moved from rhetoric to enforcement. Singapore is scrutinising exports of China-banned Nvidia chips to Malaysia [62], after silicon smugglers were arrested [63], and China's own list now names 15 US companies [56]. The chips are still reaching China: Chinese firms are getting Nvidia's Blackwell chips by ordering through nearby countries [64], which defies US bans [65]. For the China block the change is the enforcement loop, which is more likely to hit technology earnings than the PMI.

Playbook ✓: Own the China internet and Hong Kong rally only in a size that can take a tariff headline, and keep yuan exposure small while USD/CNY sits at 7.2843 and rising. Add on pullbacks toward the 20-session reference levels rather than chasing, because the Hang Seng's 10.35 percent gain is the entry risk. The call changes if the March 10 retaliation [54] is followed by new export-control listings, which would put technology supply chains back at the front of the trade. ⚠ Divergence: equities price stimulus that the 0.5 percent consumer inflation reading [40] and the property decline do not yet confirm.

Macro Stance: The Bank of Japan has a hiking bias that tariffs have not removed. Japan's inflation reached a two-year high of 4 percent in January [66], and the headlines frame the hike path as still the base case [67]. Core inflation in the capital hit a one-year high [68], and food prices are harder for the bank to overlook [69]. The governor warned of strong global uncertainty from US tariffs [70], so the bank is weighing rising prices against a tariff shock that is slowing the economy. Corporate capex fell for the first time in four years as tariff fears grew [71].

Activity & Currency: USD/JPY closed at 149.3, down 0.97 percent in the prior session and down 3.85 percent over 20 sessions from 155.28 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). The Nikkei 225 closed at 37,331.18, down 1.2 percent in the prior session and 5.66 percent over 20 sessions. Traders placed a record bet on a rising yen [72], and speculative interest in the rally has been unprecedented [73]; the yen is near a four-month high on US Treasury yields [74]. The exporter read-through is harsh, with US auto tariffs threatening a heavy blow to Japanese exports [75].

Playbook ✓: Stay underweight Tokyo's exporters and chip-equipment names into the tariff and yen squeeze. Tokyo Electron is down 14.33 percent over 20 sessions and Advantest down 10.2 percent (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). Own the yen tactically while USD/JPY stays below its 155.28 reference from 4 February. A move back above that level would say the rate-hike bet is fading and the exporter trade is back in play.

Macro Stance: Australia is running on housing and the rate cut rather than exports. Reuters reports the housing market has ended its downturn as the cut lifted sentiment [76]. The Reserve Bank's own warning is that weak incomes and high inflation could follow if productivity lags [77]. Politics adds noise: the AFR argues Treasurer Jim Chalmers has damaged the RBA's independence [78], which matters for the rate path. The external signal is the currency, which sold off on the tariff escalation [79].

Demand & Financing: AUD/USD closed at 0.6216, down 1.93 percent over five sessions and flat over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). The ASX 200 closed at 8,198.10, down 0.58 percent in the prior session and 2.1 percent over 20 sessions. Financing is the pinch point: listed companies are slashing payouts in what the AFR calls a dividend horror story [80], and iron ore logged a monthly loss on China steel export concerns [81]. The RBA's index of commodity prices for February was published into that weakness [82].

Playbook ✓: Own housing-linked lenders only on dips, and keep ASX exposure to dividend-stable names. The view changes if AUD/USD breaks below 0.62 with iron ore weak, which would confirm the tariff hit reaching the commodity channel. A firm housing print with the Aussie holding its 0.6217 February reference would argue the rate cut is working through to demand.

Macro Stance: The central bank is the story. Bloomberg reported the zloty surging to a 10-year high against the dollar on a hawkish central bank [83]. Inflation is the bank's problem: one Polish headline says inflation will rise further and makes a strong case for the monetary council on rates [84], after January CPI edged up [85] and the start of the year brought a negative inflation surprise [86]. Growth is accelerating but below expectations [87]; GDP grew 2.9 percent in 2024, beating forecasts [88], and the finance minister calls it a turning-point year [89]. Wages rose strongly in 2024 [90], but industrial output is weak [91]. The labour data disagree: the domestic jobless rate is rising [92], while TVN24 reports that Poland and Czechia have the lowest unemployment in the EU [93].

Markets: USD/PLN closed at 3.9664, down 0.96 percent in the prior session and 3.10 percent over 20 sessions, and EUR/PLN closed at 4.1585, down 1.63 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). Equities took the tariff hit: the WIG20 total-return tracker fell 3.93 percent in the session to 47.48 zloty, PKO Bank Polski fell 5.66 percent to 65.96 zloty and Pekao fell 5.47 percent to 161.50. A Business Insider Polska headline says Poland stands out on the downside as markets crash on Trump's tariffs [94]. The bond side is steadier: yields fell and the zloty held stable [95], and foreign central banks are buying Polish Treasuries [96], with more than ten of them holding the bonds [97]. Stock-picking still works outside the banks: Orlen is up 14.64 percent over 20 sessions at 62.16 zloty, Dino Polska up 8.49 percent at 488.10 and mBank up 13.28 percent at 708.00 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04).

Fiscal & Politics: Fiscal policy is contested. Leszek Balcerowicz criticised the government for spending that makes no sense [98], while the finance minister says the economy is accelerating [89]. Defence is the fiscal priority, with the president vowing to spend 4.7 percent of GDP on defence this year [99]. The presidential race is the political variable: an opinion poll says a pro-Kremlin candidate could reach the second round [100], and the field has become a three-horse race [101]. A PiS billboard affair with alleged losses of 12 million zloty has gone to prosecutors [102]. Politico reports Poland's nationalists are sticking to Trump like glue ahead of the presidential election [103], a policy-risk line the zloty has to absorb.

Corporate & Sectors: Orlen is the cash engine. Its results delivered a record profit [104], and the board recommended a dividend that could be the highest in the company's history [105]; Orlen also agreed carbon-capture development with Equinor [106]. Banks are the drag on the day: Pekao made 6.4 billion zloty and wants half of it for dividends [107], but bank stocks were among the biggest decliners on Tuesday's tariff sell-off. KGHM's mines have had a series of tremors [108], and Dino set an all-time record in a weak market [109]. PZU named Andrzej Klesyk as its new chief executive [110], and Benefit Systems placed five-year bonds with demand above 1.6 billion zloty [111].

Geopolitics & Security: Security spending anchors the policy. Poland leases eight Apache gunships [112] and has revealed the cost of Starlink terminals for Ukraine [113]; Airbus and Boeing are both angling for a Polish tanker aircraft deal [114]. Russian operatives were found to have paid for anti-government graffiti in Poland [115], and the space agency is investigating a cyberattack on its systems [116]. Wałęsa's remarks on Trump's treatment of Zelenskyy [117] are the political echo of the same story.

New / Most Important: The signal that matters is foreign central-bank demand for Polish Treasuries [96], with more than ten central banks holding the bonds [97]. That flow is the bond-side reason the yield decline and the zloty's strength have held, and it stands against the equity sell-off in the banks [94]. A second signal is the euro: Bankier reports the euro is back at 4.20 zloty [118], which would matter for the banks' margin story if the rate path turns. That is a cash signal rather than a headline one, which is why it outweighs the tariff-driven bank sell-off.

Playbook ✓: Hold the zloty-bond exposure and the hawkish-NBP trade on pullbacks, and prefer Orlen and the dividend payers over the banks until the rate path is clearer. The call changes if EUR/PLN closes back above 4.20 with the bond rally intact, which would mean the currency is weakening into the tariff shock. ⚠ Divergence: bank stocks are falling on the tariff tape even as the currency and bond markets read the central bank as hawkish, so the banks are where the story and the price disagree.

Narrative: Consensus says AI spending keeps technology earnings ahead of the market, and the tape is testing that. The sector ETF closed at 218.50, down 4.04 percent over 20 sessions and 4.38 percent over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). CNBC reports tech stocks are down 7 percent since Trump's inauguration as the trade war fuels uncertainty [119]. The driver that matters now is whether hyperscaler and chip demand holds through tariffs, not whether AI demand exists.

Reported: Nvidia's results set the reference point. Sales grew 78 percent on AI demand with strong guidance [120], but the shares fell as Reuters reported the optimistic forecast failed to convince Wall Street [121]. Snowflake posted a big beat and the stock jumped [122]. CrowdStrike beat fourth-quarter earnings and revenue estimates [123], and Dell's full-year EPS beat [124] came with a dividend increase of 18 percent and a 10 billion dollar buyback [125].

EPS Upside Watch: The setup favours names with buybacks and cut expectations rather than a broad beat. Dell's buyback is shrinking its share count, and Oracle's analyst upgrade is the sell-side tilt to watch [126]. The upside case is the Stargate revenue opportunity, which the market has not priced [127]. Nvidia's stock is 8.40 percent lower over five sessions despite the sales surge, so the bar is set by margins rather than the top line.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Nvidia rebounded after the sell-off [128] and climbed back above a 3 trillion dollar market cap [129], which cuts against a sector narrative of exhausted AI demand. Analysts are not in agreement: one downgrade cited AI market concerns [130], and the tape is pricing a rotation rather than a collapse.

Narrative: Communication services are being sold on AI-capex doubts and political cost. The sector ETF closed at 100.18, down 2.36 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). Meta closed at 640.00 dollars, down 8.24 percent over 20 sessions, and Alphabet closed at 170.92, down 15.06 percent over the same stretch. The narrative is still that advertising and AI assistants can carry the sector, and the price is saying the cost of getting there is rising.

Reported: Warner Bros. Discovery added 6.4 million Max subscribers and forecast 150 million by the end of 2026 [131]. Paramount reported record subscriber growth on its fourth-quarter call [132]. Meta boosted executive bonuses to 200 percent while cutting 5 percent of its workforce [133], a cost story rather than a revenue beat.

EPS Upside Watch: Meta is the name with a dated product catalyst: a standalone Meta AI app is reported to debut during the second quarter [134]. The cost cuts [133] give the margin a cushion if the app lands. The set-up is about the product calendar rather than a beat already in hand, and the stock is already 8.24 percent lower over 20 sessions.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Product momentum is improving while the stock falls. Google's Gemini can now be reached from the iPhone's lock screen [135], and Alphabet is 15.06 percent lower over 20 sessions. The convention break is that consumer AI distribution is getting better while the market charges the sector for capex and regulation, not for product.

Narrative: The consensus is that banks benefit from a steeper curve and lighter rules, and the tape disagrees. The sector ETF closed at 49.92, down 3.52 percent in the prior session and 2.61 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). Regional banks fell 3.5 percent in the session, and Goldman Sachs closed at 581.14, down 8.10 percent over 20 sessions. Barron's says JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and other bank and brokerage stocks were hammered and sending a warning [136].

Reported: Goldman Sachs beat full-year expectations [137], and BNY Mellon beat on revenue but was in line on EPS [138]. Ready Capital's shares plunged 28 percent after a fourth-quarter loss and a dividend cut [139], a credit-cost signal in the group. Goldman is also reported to be cutting under-performing vice presidents in its latest round of layoffs [140].

EPS Upside Watch: Trading revenue is the lever in a volatile tape. Goldman's own warning that the S&P 500 rally may falter after a 5 percent selloff [141] points to desk revenue rising with volatility, which is the bank case if the drawdown continues. The risk is that the same volatility lifts provisions.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Credit is signalling the opposite of the bank-beat narrative. Credit spreads are on their longest widening streak since 2023 [142], and the bank stocks are falling even as the earnings beat. The convention break is that the bank tape prices the credit cycle, not the reported quarter.

Narrative: The oil premium has broken. WTI closed at 68.26 dollars, down 6.70 percent over 20 sessions, and Brent at 71.04 dollars (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). The XLE energy ETF is at 86.97, down 1.38 percent over 20 sessions. OPEC+ is adding barrels: the cartel agreed to raise output from April [143], after what OilPrice calls its first output hike since 2022 [144]. The narrative of a supply-shock premium is losing to a supply-add story.

Reported: Aramco posted a drop in full-year profit and cut its dividend [145], a global read on the energy margin. EOG Resources fell on lower 2025 free cash flow despite a fourth-quarter profit beat [146]. The reported numbers give the sector guidance pressure rather than upside.

EPS Upside Watch: Refiners have the cleaner set-up. US refiners will take a hit from tariffs [147], but fuel inventories could fall to a 25-year low as refinery shutdowns outpace demand [148], which supports refining spreads even as crude weakens. The upside watch is downstream, not upstream.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Crude is falling while the US refining case tightens: the margin story cuts against the crude story. The US ordered a wind-down of Chevron's oil exports from Venezuela [149], a supply removal that has not lifted prices, with WTI still down 6.70 percent over 20 sessions.

Narrative: Industrials trade as a tariff proxy. The sector ETF closed at 131.77, down 3.80 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). Caterpillar fell 9.63 percent over 20 sessions to 326.75 dollars, Boeing fell 9.65 percent to 158.90, and the aerospace and defence ETF ITA is down 4.75 percent over the same stretch. Tariff exposure is the common thread, and the market is pricing machinery and aircraft supply chains as the first casualties.

Reported: Boeing made a management change that analysts see as key to profitability [150]. ANA ordered $14 billion of jets from Boeing, Airbus and Embraer [151], but a Turkish Airlines Boeing order could take six more months [152]. Rolls-Royce hit an all-time high on an upbeat outlook and a profit beat [153], a UK read-through for the aerospace supply chain.

EPS Upside Watch: Earnings momentum sits in Europe rather than the US primes. Thales soared as its 2024 earnings beat forecasts on defence spending [154], and the European defence bid is being backed by orders. The US names have the tariff overhang on their margins instead.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Europe's defence spend is rising while US defence stocks fall. The ITA ETF is down 4.75 percent over 20 sessions even as Europe announced a $840 billion rearmament plan [32]. The split between the two sides of the Atlantic is the convention break in this group.

Narrative: The consumer story is tariff pass-through. The sector ETF closed at 208.24, down 9.11 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). Best Buy's chief executive said price increases are highly likely because of the Trump tariffs [155], and Target braces for first-quarter profit pressure from tariffs and low demand [156]. The narrative is that the consumer absorbs the price rise, and the stock tape says the consumer will not absorb it cheaply.

Reported: Target's sales fell but its earnings topped expectations [157], and its shares wobbled: 8.05 percent lower over five sessions at 117.14 dollars. Best Buy's shares slumped on its price-hike warning [158]. AutoZone missed quarterly revenue estimates on inflation and currency rates [159], while Nordstrom beat holiday-quarter sales estimates [160].

EPS Upside Watch: Nordstrom's holiday-quarter beat [160] is the cleanest beat in the group. The EPS bar elsewhere is set by guidance into tariffs, which the sector has not yet cut, so the upside watch is for the names that reset guidance first rather than those that beat the last quarter.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Tesla is the convention break in the group. China-made EV sales fell to their lowest since August 2022 [161], and the stock is down 29.10 percent over 20 sessions to 272.04 dollars (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). Morgan Stanley still sees the stock reaching 430 dollars and reinstated it as a top pick [162].

Narrative: Defensives are the rotation of the week. The sector ETF closed at 82.10, up 3.54 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04), while the cyclicals are down. Coca-Cola is up 10.80 percent over 20 sessions at 70.19 dollars, PepsiCo up 2.61 percent at 154.19 and Procter & Gamble up 2.62 percent at 173.18. The narrative is recession insurance, and the price is buying it.

Reported: Monster Beverage missed its fourth-quarter estimates [163], and shoppers turning to smaller food brands cut into Unilever and P&G profits [164]. The reported numbers are weaker than the price, which is why the sector is a rotation trade rather than an earnings one.

EPS Upside Watch: The staples set-up is a defensive re-rating rather than an earnings beat. The names with pricing power lead, and Coca-Cola's 10.80 percent 20-session gain shows the market paying for it. The risk is margin pressure from cheaper private-label and smaller brands [164], which would show up at the next print.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Staples are rising while the consumer discretionary names fall, and that is the break. Walmart, the consumer's bellwether, is down 4.59 percent over 20 sessions at 94.97 dollars even as the defensive sector gains. The rotation is into the sector, not into the big-box retailers.

Narrative: Obesity drugs carry the health-care narrative. Eli Lilly closed at 911.06 dollars, up 12.42 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04), while UnitedHealth is down 13.42 percent over 20 sessions at 474.61 dollars after its full-year EPS missed expectations [165]. The sector is split between a growth drug story and a managed-care cost story.

Reported: UnitedHealth's full-year EPS missed [165]. Viatris plummeted on a disappointing fourth quarter and 2025 outlook [166], and Teladoc tumbled on a wider-than-expected loss and disappointing guidance [167]. The misses cluster in managed care and specialty names, not in the large drugmakers.

EPS Upside Watch: Lilly's set-up is pipeline spend. It has stockpiled nearly $550 million of its next obesity drug [168] and is taking aim at copycats with a new advertising campaign [169], which signals a defended franchise rather than a surprise. The upside watch is the volume of the franchise, not a single quarter.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Pfizer could use existing US manufacturing to counter a potential tariff hit [170], which means the tariff risk is being hedged inside the sector. The market is still selling the managed-care names, with UnitedHealth down 13.42 percent over 20 sessions, so the sector's hedging is not the same as the price.

Narrative: Materials are split between a copper bid and a steel slump. The sector ETF closed at 85.80, down 3.47 percent over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-04). Copper is up 5.44 percent over 20 sessions at 4.53 dollars a pound, supported by grid and AI data-centre build-out, as the industry needs $2.1 trillion of investment over the next 25 years [171].
